title: Say inshallah
hookLine: never say I'll do it tomorrow without, if Allah wills (18:23–24)

cards: See you at eight, inshallah. The test is Thursday, inshallah. We'll finish the kitchen by spring, inshallah.
If you have Muslim friends or coworkers, you've heard it tacked onto plans so often it sounds like punctuation. Some people even joke that it's a polite way of saying probably not.
But the word comes from the middle of al-Kahf, and it arrived, the biographies say, after an awkward silence.

teach.h: THREE QUESTIONS; I'LL TELL YOU TOMORROW.
teach.b: Here's the story as Ibn Ishaq's biography tells it; it's from the sirah, not from the Qur'an or the major hadith collections.

The Quraysh in Mecca put three questions to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: about young men who disappeared long ago, about a great traveler, and about the spirit. He said: I'll tell you tomorrow. He didn't add: if God wills.
Tomorrow came, and no revelation. Nor the next day.
By this account the wait lasted around fifteen days, and the people of Mecca mocked him.
When the answer came, it included this, in Pickthall's words: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." In Arabic: in sha' Allah. If God wills.
Three words that became one. The verse isn't banning plans. You're still meant to say I'll do it tomorrow.
It adds the honest clause: the future isn't in your hands, and every plan is made inside a will larger than yours. Then: remember your Lord when you forget.

teach.h: FORGOT? SAY IT WHEN YOU REMEMBER.
teach.b: If you made a plan and forgot to say it, say it when you remember. No penalty, no guilt; just come back.

And the end of the verse: say, perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right than this. So inshallah isn't meant to be a polite no. Scholars have long said it should go with a real intention to do the thing.
It's a yes, held with open hands.

how: Muslims say inshallah when speaking of any future plan, following 18:23–24; many scholars teach that it should accompany a sincere intention, and that if forgotten, it can be said on remembering.

o: a polite way of saying probably not
if God wills, said with a real plan
a prayer for luck before a journey

games.q: you're asked three hard questions and you say, I'll tell you tomorrow. tomorrow comes and you have no answer. what happens in Ibn Ishaq's account?
o: the answer comes the next morning.
about fifteen days of silence, then revelation that includes 'except if Allah will.'
games.why: the wait lasts around fifteen days in this account, and the answer comes with the instruction to say inshallah.

practice: Run through your plans for tomorrow, the meetings, the errands, the call you've been meaning to make, and as each one comes up, add the clause: inshallah if you're Muslim, or the plain meaning, if it's given to me.
Notice how each plan feels with it attached: lighter, less certain, more honest. Don't drop any plans; just hold each one a little more loosely.

wordCard.voice: Say inshallah. If God wills: three Arabic words become one, attached to every tomorrow, a real yes held with open hands. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: if God wills (18:24). Often written as one word in English: inshallah.

carryVoice: Your line: if allah wills. The plan stays, and the clause keeps it honest. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will.
